cards.title: THE WORKSHOP
cards.tagline: SIX ZONES. START AT SAFETY, EVEN THOUGH IT IS THE SMALLEST.
cards.objective: The workshop is the room 6S came from, and the only one in the house where a bad standard can cost you a finger rather than an afternoon. This card is the map.
cards.start_here: WSZ-006 Safety and PPE Station. Take the Safety and PPE Station first even though it is the smallest zone in the room. It sets the terms for the other five: once the glasses hang by the door and the extinguisher gauge reads green, you can work through the blades and the solvents without improvising.
how_to_play: 1. Deal the six ZONE cards face up. Start at Safety and PPE Station, or take the zone that is annoying you today.
2. Lay out that zone's three FRICTION cards. Keep the ones that are true in your workshop. Put the rest back.
3. Turn a friction card over and pick the answer that is true. It names a ROOT CAUSE.
4. The root cause card names the ACTION cards that fix that cause. Pick the one that matches the time you actually have: fifteen or thirty minutes.
5. Do it standing up, with the card in your hand.
6. Read the victory condition out loud. If it is not true yet, you are not finished, and that is the whole scoring system.
7. Fill in the zone's STANDARD card with a pen and put it where the zone is.
8. Draw an EVENT card when an ordinary hard day happens, and see whether the standard held.
cards.players: 1 to 2. A shared shop runs on the same standards for everyone who uses it: the visitor rule on the Safety and PPE Station card exists precisely because two people improvising two different rules is how someone gets hurt.
cards.six_s: Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, Sustain
cards.safety_first: Do WSA-013 The Full Workshop Hazard Walk before any rebuild. It takes thirty minutes and covers every stuck guard, the unanchored small-parts cabinet and material rack, a shallow-leaning sheet good, the extinguisher gauge, and any loose oily rag.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: Chisels and marking knives lying edge up in an open tray, and a vise whose jaws have worn smooth enough to release a workpiece mid-cut.

safety_checks.question: Water and electricity
safety_checks.text: The task lamp or a tool cord running across the bench or down onto a damp concrete floor where you stand to work.

the_call.title: The project that has been on the bench since spring
the_call.text: You have a half-assembled something occupying your best surface, and you have not touched it in months because the next step is one you are unsure how to do. Here is the rule that settles it: say out loud what the next physical action is and what date this month you will do it. If you cannot name both in one breath, the project is finished. Take it apart, put the hardware back in the fastener drawers, put the stock back on the rack, and let the bench go back to being a bench. Keeping it assembled is not keeping the project alive, it is only keeping the surface unusable.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: A blade guard that has stopped springing shut on its own, and loose blades stored flat in a drawer where your hand goes in first.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: Lithium battery packs left on chargers indefinitely, especially sitting on a wooden shelf under a bench full of sawdust.

the_call.title: The expensive tool you never use
the_call.text: Somewhere in this zone is a tool that cost real money and has not cut anything in two years, and you keep it because selling it would be admitting the purchase was wrong. Two questions settle it. Has it done work in the last twenty-four months? And if the job came up tomorrow, would you happily hire one for a day instead? If the answer is no and yes, sell it now, while it still fetches something and while the batteries in it are still worth having. A tool losing value on your shelf is not an asset you are holding, it is a decision you are storing.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: A loaded small-parts cabinet pulling off the wall, or a top-heavy drawer unit tipping when you open the highest drawer full of bolts.

the_call.title: The inherited jar of mixed hardware
the_call.text: There is a jar or a tin, probably from a relative's garage, holding a few kilograms of unsorted screws, nuts, and washers, and it has followed you through two houses because there is obviously good hardware in there. Price the alternative first: a full box of the screws you actually drive costs less than the evening you would spend sorting. So give it one sitting. Pick out only the sizes you already have a compartment for, and when the sitting ends, whatever is left in the jar goes to metal recycling that same day. Do not tip the remainder back into a smaller jar. That is exactly how it survived the last two moves.

cards.title: MATERIAL RACK
cards.tagline: ONE OFFCUT BIN. A SIZE FLOOR AND A FILL LINE, BOTH WRITTEN ON.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: Sheet goods sliding off a shallow lean, and long boards pulled from the middle of a stack bringing the ones above down onto your feet.

the_call.title: The offcut that is still good wood
the_call.text: This is the hardest decision in the workshop and you already know it. Every short piece in that bin is genuinely usable, which is exactly why the pile never shrinks, and the cost of keeping it is invisible while the cost of tossing it feels sharp. Set two limits and let them decide for you instead. A size floor, anything shorter than your forearm or narrower than your palm, and a bin cap, one bin and no overflow. When the bin is full, the shortest piece in it leaves to make room for the newest. You are not judging whether a piece is good wood. You are only judging whether it is better than the worst piece already in the bin.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: Oil finish rags balled up in a bin liner or draped over the bench, and solvent stored within reach of a water heater flame.

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
safety_checks.text: Thinner or turpentine decanted into an unlabeled drink bottle, and spraying or brushing solvent based finish in a closed shop with the door shut.

the_call.title: The wall of half-used paint
the_call.text: You are storing a row of part cans against the possibility of a touch-up, including colors from a wall you painted over and a house you no longer live in. Almost none of it will still brush out matching in two years anyway. So keep only colors currently on a surface in this house, and keep them properly: one small sealed jar of each, labeled with the room and the finish, not the original half-empty tin sitting open to the air. Everything else goes to hazardous waste on the same day you sort it, because a box of condemned paint sitting by the door for a month is just the same problem, relocated.

supplies: Mineral spirits or matching brush cleaner

cards.title: SAFETY AND PPE STATION
cards.tagline: A FULL BOARD AT THE DOOR. ONE LABELED SET PER USER.
cards.objective: Make protective gear so easy to reach that putting it on is faster than skipping it.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: An extinguisher with the gauge out of the green, no inspection date on it, or a stack of timber leaning against the wall in front of it.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: Safety glasses so scratched that you take them off to see the cut line, which is the moment the chip flies.

the_call.title: The visitor rule
the_call.text: The genuinely awkward decision here is not your own gear, it is what happens when your brother-in-law or your fourteen year old wanders in while the saw is running and wants to help. You have been handling it case by case, which means you have been handling it badly. Decide it once and hang it on the wall: anyone who works in this shop has their own labeled set of glasses and muffs, and there is one spare set on a hook marked for visitors. If a visitor will not wear it, they stay on the near side of the doorway and watch. Saying that once, in advance, is far easier than saying it while holding a running grinder.

cards.tagline: WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE. THEN WHY.
cards.objective: A full sheet of plywood is leaning against the wall at a shallow angle instead of standing close to vertical.

cards.title: CAN THE LOOSE RAGS AND DATE THE OPEN LIDS
cards.objective: Put every loose oil-finish rag into the lidded metal can with the lid down, and date any open can on the shelf that is missing one.
cards.why_it_matters: A balled up oil rag generates its own heat as it cures and can ignite with nothing touching it, and an undated can is how a finish quietly skins over before you notice.
steps: Check every rag from today's finishing work: anything balled up loose goes into the lidded metal can with the lid pushed down, and scan the open cans on the shelf for one without a date and mark it now.

cards.title: KEEP ONLY THE COLORS STILL ON A WALL AND SEPARATE THE SHELVES
cards.objective: Narrow the paint shelf down to only colors currently on a surface in this house, in small sealed jars, and put solvents and water based finishes on separate shelves.
cards.why_it_matters: Almost none of an old can will brush out matching in two years anyway, and solvents sharing a shelf with water based finish is the actual incompatible-storage hazard this zone exists to prevent.
steps: Decant a small sealed, labeled jar of each color still on a wall in this house, and take every other can straight to household hazardous waste that same day.
Move every solvent and thinner onto its own shelf, separate from water based paint, with the layout written on the inside of the cabinet door.

cards.title: CHECK THE EXTINGUISHER AND CULL THE SCRATCHED GLASSES
cards.objective: Lift the extinguisher and confirm the gauge sits in the green, then bin any pair of safety glasses scratched enough to tempt you to lift them off mid-cut.
cards.why_it_matters: A dead extinguisher looks identical to a working one until the moment you need it, and a scratched pair you lift off mid-cut is the exact moment the chip flies.
inputs: masking tape and a marker for the date

cards.title: SET THE VISITOR RULE AND MATCH THE BOARD TO THE SHORTEST USER
cards.objective: Decide the visitor rule once and hang it on the wall, and lower or add a hook so the shortest regular user can reach their own gear without help.
cards.why_it_matters: Handling the visitor question case by case means handling it badly, and a hook board mounted to the tallest user's height means the shortest one skips the gear because reaching for it is a hassle.
inputs: a marker and a card for the wall
steps: Write the visitor rule on a card and hang it at the door: anyone who works in this shop gets a labeled set, one spare set is marked for visitors, and anyone who will not wear it stays on the near side of the doorway.
Check the shortest regular user can reach their own hook without stretching or asking for help, and add or lower a hook if they cannot.
